newsitem.title: UK: Pan-Euro power trade seen unlikely for several years.
newsitem.headline: Pan-Euro power trade seen unlikely for several years.

text.p: A European electricity market looks unlikely for some years, despite the formulation of the the EU's Electricity Directive six months ago after years of wrangling, an industry conference was told on Wednesday.
"I don't believe there is one and I think it is unlikely there will be for quite a while yet," said Richard Tomiak, general manager of electricity purchasing at Midlands Electricity.
"Clearly there are many national power markets and their number is increasing, but they are all distinct and largely separate," he said.

As well as great diversity between the development of market structures in different EU member states, cross-border interconnections are not sufficient to support physical trade between countries, he said.
But lack of a physical link, while ruling out selling physical output to another country, does not prevent the development of instruments such as derivatives to allow hedging between markets.

Tomiak said such hedging would involve a high level of risk if the market circumstances and prices in the two different countries are widely different, but a relatively low risk if the markets are closely correlated.
Under the electricity directive, EU members must introduce competition progressively into the electricity sector.
They must open 22.5 percent of their markets initially, rising to 28.5 percent by 2000 and 33 percent by 2006. These levels are in place from January 1997, but not legally enforceable until 1999.
Although large energy users welcome the directive as a step towards full competition and lower prices, Tomiak said that some see the directive as "extremely disappointing."

This is partly because supply companies from countries which liberalise their markets slowly will be able to penetrate competitors' markets while reciprocal access to their own markets will be limited.

But although the directive will give large energy users in member states the freedom to choose their own suppliers - and in some countries like Britain, small consumers as well - Tomiak said the directive will not in itself lead to the development of a single European market.

"It is clear that some countries - the United Kingdom and Sweden - have already privatised and deregulated their electricity industries, while several others, Spain, Holland, Germany, even Italy are well on their way to full market liberalisation," he said.
But he added that France is lagging behind and Belgium, Ireland and Greece, with relatively small electricity sectors, have been allowed to delay implementation of the directive.

Capital costs in construction of new plant are becoming standardised across Europe, as are costs for the major generation fuels such as oil, coal, gas and uranium, so there are factors standardising electricity prices even while the structure of markets varies from one country to another, he said.

But because electricity generating companies have only operated in their own local markets until now, Tomiak believes that they are unlikely to have the expertise to take advantage of cross-border hedging and arbitrage opportunities.
Instead, he believed, traders and brokers already specialising in risk management are likely to take on this role.
